The Generalized Riemann Hypothesis is easier to understand than you might think On November 20 the Riemann Hypothesis, the most famous unsolved problem in mathematics, was proven by the mathematician Levent Alpöge working with Claude. The generalized version they proved can be understood without complex analysis, using mathematics any computer science student knows

Two adjacent Bluesky posts independently make the same observation: AI models can excel at formal problems and still stumble over messy real-world context.

Alex Becker (@alexbecker.net): “working with strong models has made me appreciate that humans are actually really well calibrated decision makers, modulo some well-known biases. wdym you can solve millennium prize problems but you are going to drop a key feature because you misread some random sentence from some doc”

hikikomorphism (@hikikomorphism.bsky.social): “LLMs have a faculty with formal systems I've taken to describing as "omni-phd", but they struggle with the messy complexity of the real world.

This leads to some non-obvious patterns and antipatterns.”

It is entirely plausible that around half of your unique long-tail senders lack DKIM. A 2022 study found DKIM enabled on only 28.1% of Alexa’s top million domains. USENIX Security study⁠�

A spectrogram, or waterfall display, on a near-black navy background, titled "WATERFALL · AT THE ANTENNA" in spaced blue capitals, with "ВОДОПАД" (Russian for "waterfall") beneath. A logarithmic frequency axis along the bottom runs from 50 Hz to 6.4 kHz (50, 100, 200, 400, 800, 1.6k, 3.2k, 6.4k), and thin corner brackets frame the top left and bottom right. Signal energy appears as pale blue streaks and blobs, with small amber-orange spots marking the strongest points. In the upper half, horizontal bands of energy begin around 150–300 Hz at the top and step steadily rightward with each row, forming a diagonal cascade that reaches about 1–2 kHz. As it descends, it breaks into ladder-like rows of repeating dots that fade toward 4 kHz. A thin, bright curved line sweeps from about 500 Hz near the top, down and to the right, to roughly 2 kHz at mid-height. Below a dark gap, a denser, speckled cluster spans roughly 600 Hz to 3 kHz. Near the bottom, a narrower band sits around 700 Hz to 1.5 kHz. A second thin curve arcs down on the right side and reaches the bottom edge near 5 kHz. Faint, blurry smears of low-frequency energy hug the far left edge below 100 Hz.

Screenshot of a dark, sci-fi navigation interface in thin blue and white type. The top bar reads "Nostalgia for Infinity · ε Eridani → δ Pavonis · RX array nominal" with a "Briefing" button. The main panel is titled "Stellar Chart · Ecliptic," with the Russian subtitle "Звёздная карта" (star map). Top-right readouts: AZ 003.0, EL 36.3, R 47.2 ly; epoch J2000, frame ecliptic; carriers in flight 03/12.

The chart is a tilted 3D star map. Concentric elliptical rings, marked 20, 25 and 30 light-years, center on Sol, labeled "Earth." Each star is a small white point on a thin vertical line dropping to the ecliptic plane. Some stars carry colony names in blue: Epsilon Eridani (Yellowstone), Delta Pavonis (Resurgam), 61 Cygni (Sky's Edge), Gliese 687 (Haven), Groombridge 1618 (Turquoise), Lalande 21258 (Zion), Ross 248 (Diadem), Lacaille 9352 (Fand) and P Eridani (Ararat). Unnamed stars include Sigma Draconis, Eta Cassiopeiae, Xi Boötis, Lalande 21185, Procyon, Wolf 359, Barnard's Star, Sirius, 40 Eridani, Tau Ceti, 70 Ophiuchi, Alpha Centauri, Epsilon Indi, 36 Ophiuchi and Beta Hydri.

Faint colored lines trace ship routes between systems. A pale line runs from Epsilon Eridani down to Delta Pavonis near the bottom of the chart, and a yellowish line runs to P Eridani. Small colored dots in pink, blue, yellow, orange, magenta and green mark ships in transit along these paths. Several labels near the center overlap.

The bottom-right hint reads "Drag to turn · Pinch or Ctrl-scroll to zoom · Click a ship." Along the bottom edge is a row of toggle buttons, partly cut off: "Corrected," "Beacon," "Pitch corr · On," "Radio · On," "Hiss · Ships," "Cabin · On" and "Depth · On."
